rationale: A wins because it gives the founder five real routes to coverage without pretending they are the same story, and the patient angle, "Patients priced out of branded weight-loss drugs now have a cheaper option — with an FDA warning attached," is a valid consumer-health shape B leaves on the table. B is disciplined, but "A newly profitable Hims & Hers bets its margins on compounded weight-loss drugs" turns a financial-risk angle into an unsupported margin claim. That is how a decent angle gets itself sued in the headline.
gaps_in_A: "branded drugmakers want it stopped" overstates the supplied fact that manufacturers "have pushed back." Pushback is not automatically a stop-the-launch campaign.
"Patients priced out of branded weight-loss drugs" is plausible but not explicitly in the update; it needs a price and a named patient before it can carry a consumer story.
The regulatory angle asks for legal basis and supplier identity, but should also demand the exact FDA flag: what was flagged, when, and whether it covers this specific compounded product.
The next step jumps to `journalist-fit-check`; for this fact pattern, source verification should come before reporter matching.
gaps_in_B: "bets its margins" is invented. The update says Hims recently turned profitable, not that this product affects margins or that management has tied profitability to GLP-1s.
"selling a compounded copy of a blockbuster drug" adds "copy" and "blockbuster" color that is not in the supplied facts. Cute, but not grounded.
"Decay: 4hr" on the FDA angle is fake precision. Nothing in the update supports a four-hour clock.

It misses a usable patient-facing affordability-versus-risk angle, then refuses only the weaker version, "Why patients are choosing compounded semaglutide over branded drugs." Correct refusal, incomplete strategy.
